source.title: Cooperative Games with Incomplete Information: Some Open Problems

accepted.question_text: How should the ex ante core be defined for cooperative games with incomplete information when strategic externalities are present, so that the definition properly accounts for the fact that the actions of players outside a coalition can affect that coalition's members' payoffs?
accepted.context_brief: Ex ante core with strategic externalities

evidence.quote: One important question, still open, is what would be appropriate definitions of the ex ante core in contexts with strategic externalities.

accepted.question_text: In exchange economies with asymmetric information at the interim stage, which negotiation procedures can support a generalized Nash program that explains coalition formation and stable payoff distribution when coalitions communicate and block allocations under incomplete information?
accepted.context_brief: Generalized Nash program under incomplete information

evidence.quote: In general, the exploration of different negotiation procedures should be an important vehicle to tackle questions of coalition formation and stable payoff distribution. These questions, comprising a generalized Nash program, remain almost entirely unexplored in these settings.

accepted.question_text: Beyond the currently known positive results for quasilinear economies and other special assumptions, what alternative economically interesting assumptions or scenarios guarantee non-emptiness of interim core concepts for exchange economies with asymmetric information, including cores defined through equilibrium blocking or related mechanism-based objections?

evidence.quote: Understanding the limitations that these and other conditions may have, the search for alternative interesting scenarios in which non-emptiness of the core obtains should also be part of the research agenda.

accepted.question_text: How do core concepts and equilibrium notions behave in large markets with asymmetric information, especially with respect to core convergence and the way information is transmitted or revealed through market interaction and blocking mechanisms?

evidence.quote: Given how important it is to understand information flows in markets, more research along these lines is definitely needed.

accepted.question_text: Can the cooperative and noncooperative characterizations obtained by de Clippel and Minelli for bargaining with verifiable types be extended to the harder setting in which players' types remain unverifiable even at the stage where the mechanism is used to make decisions?

evidence.quote: An obvious open problem is the extension of these results when types remain unverifiable, even at the decision stage.

accepted.question_text: How can the cooperative-competitive (coco) solution for Bayesian games with transferable utility be extended from the two-player case to settings with more than two players?
accepted.context_brief: Coco value for more than two players

evidence.quote: A. Kalai and E. Kalai (2011) point out the following open problems: extension of the coco value in the TU case for more than two players and in the NTU case for two players or more, and construction of a second best analog of the coco value for environments that do not satisfy ex post observability conditions.

accepted.question_text: How can the cooperative-competitive (coco) solution be extended to non-transferable-utility Bayesian games, for either two players or larger groups of players?
accepted.context_brief: Coco value for NTU Bayesian games

evidence.quote: A. Kalai and E. Kalai (2011) point out the following open problems: extension of the coco value in the TU case for more than two players and in the NTU case for two players or more, and construction of a second best analog of the coco value for environments that do not satisfy ex post observability conditions.

accepted.question_text: In environments where types or payoffs do not satisfy the ex post observability assumptions used to obtain first-best implementation results, can one construct a second-best analog of the coco solution that remains appropriate under incomplete information?
accepted.context_brief: Second-best coco without ex post observability

evidence.quote: A. Kalai and E. Kalai (2011) point out the following open problems: extension of the coco value in the TU case for more than two players and in the NTU case for two players or more, and construction of a second best analog of the coco value for environments that do not satisfy ex post observability conditions.

accepted.question_text: For Bayesian noncooperative games with coalitions of intermediate size, how should one formulate meaningful incentive-compatibility conditions for a coalition S with 2 < |S| < |N|, given that internal incentives depend on threats and the coalition's ability to commit to threats depends on its members' private information?

evidence.quote: The formulation of meaningful incentive compatibility conditions for coalitions S (such that 2 < |S| < |N|) in a Bayesian noncooperative game can be a real challenge. In the absence of an ad hoc scenario, we face a circular problem since incentives inside a coalition should take into account the commitments to threats, and the ability of a coalition to commit to threats depends on its members’ information.

accepted.question_text: Can the core-based results obtained for Bayesian games with transferable utility under independent private values and ex ante coalition commitment be extended when one relaxes either the independent-private-values assumption, the ex ante coalition-commitment assumption, or both?
accepted.context_brief: Relaxing IPV and ex ante commitment assumptions

evidence.quote: Independent private values in the basic game G and ex ante commitment of coalitions play a crucial role in the previous results and relaxation of these assumptions is an obvious topic for future research.
